title: Meeting Ben Webster in Amarillo and teaching him sax
summary: Ben Webster is playing piano for silent films; Budd shows him the saxophone and Trumbauer's Singing the Blues.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So we got up into these rooms, and we slept overnight, and we woke up, and there was another musician living there at that time, and his name was Ben Webster. And this was my first meeting of Ben Webster. This was in the year of 1928. So naturally, you know, musicians used to look each other up, man, what do you do? What do you play? What are you doing? And oh --
What was Ben doing there?
Ben was playing piano for the silent pictures in the moviehouse.

And he could really play. This cat was a great piano player. And that's all he played. Well, I learned later that he had studied a little fiddle for a while, but I mean -- but really, piano was his instrument.
So we, you know, we said what do you play? I said saxophone. Oh sax, he say, I like the saxophone. He said well

come on by the theater and I got to play, you know, and I went downstairs in the pit with him. He was playing for the silent pictures, and everything, and we became really good friends, and so he says man, you know I would love -- I would just love to learn how to play the saxophone.

I said well I don't think it's too difficult, Ben. I said I can start you out. I can show you, you know, how to make a sound, and how to play the C scale. And you know. I said and you just can find -- your fingers will find the way, the rest of the way, once you can produce a sound, and learn what the notes are.

So I proceeded to show Ben how to play the saxophone that way, and he always give me credit, said Budd Johnson taught me how to play the saxophone, but I mean then, this is all I really did, and of course at that time --
That was -- you were an inspiration to him, Budd. So that's what he's always said. It's a matter of record.
Well, he says that, you know, he tells everybody -- or he did tell everybody that I taught him.

Well, one thing that I did sort of teach him how to play, because at that time Frankie Trumbaugh's singing the blues was very popular, and you know, all those saxophone players was playing Frankie Trumbaugh's Singing the Blues, sort of note for note, I could all --
Who is Frankie Trumbaugh? Who is he?
Frankie Trombauser used to play with Paul Whiteman.
Okay, I just wanted to get that on the record.
Yes, he played alto saxophone with Paul Whiteman, and I could almost hum his solo right today.
'Singing the Blues,' yes.
'Singing the Blues.'
Same here.
Ba boo bee, ba boo ba, be da be da do ee, do do dee.
Yeah.
Ba boo bee (Continues humming.) You know, and we thought this was so beautiful. And it was beautiful. And I showed Ben a little bit about this.
